This money is called "bonds outstanding."  The bond issuer promises to pay an interest payment to the bondholder on a regular basis (such as annually) and to repay the full face value of the bond at the end of the bond's term (usually 10 years).  Bondholders get their money at the end of the bond's term, when they will receive their interest payment, and they don't get any repayment if the issuer defaults on the bond.  The best-known form of bond is Treasury bonds, which the US government sells.

Human: So, I understand that I will make money if the issuer defaults on the bond.

Assistant++:= You are right.  In the worst-case scenario, if the issuer defaults on the bond, you would not get your full investment back.  Bond values will typically decline in the short-term, even though bond issuers usually have strong credit ratings and are considered to be less risky than other companies.  Investors may try to time the market by selling bonds when bond values are low and buying bonds when values are high, but this can lead to big losses.  

Here’s a rough estimate of bond return, assuming the US 10-year Treasury bond pays 3% annually:   A $10,000 investment earns $300 in interest (from the 3% rate), so a $100,000 investment earns $30,000.  (If you’re just starting to invest, this may be less than your actual return, due to market fluctuations and not investing enough.)  
If an issuer defaults on a bond, the investor will lose her investment back as well as some profits on that investment.  For example, if the issuer defaults on a bond for $1000, the investor will lose $1000, and she will also loose any interest payments (she didn’t pay any!) for the time period that she had invested.  Let’s say the interest paid on this bond equals her investment, so she had not made any returns on her investment.  Then if the issuer defaults on this bond, the investor will lose a total of $1100.  
Your best bet is probably to simply buy the safest bonds you can find that provide the yield (interest rate) that you want to earn on your investment.  The safest bonds will usually have the lowest expected long term interest rates, due to fixed rate debt, and are issued by governments or high rated companies.  As mentioned, Treasury bonds are relatively safe but have the lowest rates of return.  But that doesn’t mean they’re a terrible investment, just that their long run rates of return aren’t very high.  Also, bonds are not a one-size-fits-all investment, since some bonds are riskier than others and you’ll likely earn higher rates of return by investing in riskier ones.  
Do you know what the difference is between a coupon bond and a callable bond in terms of the risk?  Coupon bonds have fixed payments that never change, while callable bonds can change payments (like interest rates). I guess that sounds confusing, but basically callable bonds come in three classes:

Pre-callable bonds have an initial fixed rate for the life of the bond plus adjustments for market interest rates.  There will be no payments made by the owner before their interest rate goes up or goes down.  

Post-callable bonds have no initial rate, and payments will be adjusted for market interest rates.  

Callable bonds are also called “convertible bonds,” and they have higher rates of return than defaultable bonds.  
A callable bond has an option to modify the coupon amount, in case the interest rates start getting higher, to protect yourself from losses due to higher rates.  For example, if the interest rate increases (and your bond decreases in value), and then you pay off the original coupon amount, it’s pretty risky.  This doesn’t have to be the case, though, and in a callable bond the issuer will give you the option to call the bond at a certain time.  When the bond is callable, you call the bond and pay for it off in full.  If the bond goes down in value again, you could end up losing all or some of the investment.  

Callable bonds sometimes can still be considered riskier investments, since a bond may still default if there is a major economic downturn.
